course_description:
The threats posed to nation states, businesses, and individuals by cybercriminals are expanding in reach and developing in their levels of sophistication. The cyber security specialist of the future must possess a working knowledge of the tools at their disposal to detect, deter, defend against, and respond to these growing threats. This course will provide working knowledge of Australian and international regulatory frameworks; the techniques and challenges associated with cybercrime investigation; and the array of criminal justice system responses that are available to address cybercrime offending. Students will be introduced to cybercrime investigation methods and the cyber attack attribution-response processes employed by national agencies. The various roles and responsibilities of national and state intelligence/law enforcement agencies for cybercrime investigation and responses will also be explored, as will questions of privacy, freedom, and security.

CRIM7090 will provide students with a working knowledge of Australian and international regulatory frameworks; the techniques and challenges associated with cybercrime investigation; and the array of criminal justice system / private sector responses that are available to address cybercrime offending. Students will be introduced to cybercrime / digital forensic investigation methods as they are applied for cyber attacks committed against individuals, businesses and national agencies. The roles and responsibilities of government and private sector agencies for cybercrime investigation and responses will also be explored, as will questions of privacy, freedom, and security. Instruction in each of the four course modules will be augmented by guest presenters from law enforcement, national security and cyber security specialists.

learning_outcomes.description: Possess a mix of theoretical and applied knowledge related to the current cyber threat landscape and the challenges confronting government, private & public sector responses to cyber crime offending in domestic and international contexts.
Understand and critically analyse the regulations, investigative techniques and responses associated with cyber crime offending against individuals.
Understand and critically analyse the regulations, investigative techniques and responses associated with cyber crime offending against the private sector / businesses.
Understand and critically analyse the regulations, investigative techniques and responses associated with cyber crime offending against the government / national agencies.

assessment_details.title: Regulatory Response Brief
assessment_details.task_description: Students will select a contemporary cybercrime issue (e.g. ransomware, online child exploitation, cryptocurrency fraud, cyber-enabled disinformation, youth and violent extremism on social media) and write a 1000 word regulatory response brief. The brief should critically evaluate current Australian regulatory and criminal justice responses to the chosen issue and make two evidence-based recommendations for improvement. This is a research exercise designed to assess student's substantive knowledge of course content and ability to present and develop a cogent argument. The brief should be written in formal academic style and in correct, grammatical, and succinct English. The brief is restricted to 1000 words in length (excluding reference list) and utilise APA 7th citation protocol. Students must use a minimum of five academic / government sources found through their own research beyond the course reading list. Suitable sources include books, book chapters, credible journal articles and Australian government policy or regulatory documents. Students may use some tertiary sources in addition to the five academic / government sources if necessary. These may include online statistics from reputable sources, newspaper articles, etc. Please remember: lecture slides, Wikipedia, and university websites that offer theoretical definitions, etc. are NOT academic sources and should NOT be used as references. The full task description and marking rubric for the exercise can be found on Blackboard//CRIM7090//Assessment//Regulatory Response Brief Use of AI: this task has been designed to be challenging, authentic, and complex. Successful completion of this assessment will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. To pass, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI tools. AI may be used only for simple tasks including spell-checking, grammar-checking, and translation. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . Read full task description Hide full task description
assessment_details.assessment_security: Open assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking.
assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
This assessment item must be submitted via Turnitin on Blackboard Ultra.
Refer to the eLearning Guides for steps on how to submit your Turnitin assignment. No emailed assessments will be accepted. Students must obtain a Digital Receipt as evidence of successful submission of their assessment.
Students must abide by the Student Code of Conduct Policy which outlines that all submitted assessment must be their own work, except where properly referenced.
If you are experiencing technical difficulties with Blackboard or Turnitin, please contact the ITS Support Team .
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
A request for an extension must be submitted as soon as it becomes evident that an extension is needed, and no later than the assessment due date and time. Please refer to the my.UQ Applying for an assessment extension page for information.
Extension requests are processed by the School of Social Science Administration Team. Course Coordinators are unable to grant extensions directly. Extensions in your final semester of study could delay your graduation to the next graduation period.
Late Extension Applications
Late applications must include supporting documentation outlining how it was impossible, or unsafe, for you to have applied by the due date and time. The School of Social Science will not accept personal statements.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Assessments will not be accepted if it is more than one week (7 calendar days) late without prior approval.

Week 2: Mod 1 - Current & Emerging Challenges Lecture, case study and group discussion.
Week 3: Mod 2 - Regulations & Responses (Individual Targets) Lecture, case study and group discussion. Learning outcomes: L02
Week 4: Mod 2 - Investigation Techniques (Individual Targets) Lecture, case study and group discussion. Learning outcomes: L02
Week 5: Guest Lecture - Individual Targets Guest lecture discussing Australian prevention strategies & investigative responses to cybercrimes targeting individuals.
Week 6: Short Answer Exercise 1 (Mod 1 & Mod 2) - In Class Assessment Short Answer Exercise 1 conducted in class under supervision
Week 7: Mod 3 - Regulations & Responses (Private Sector Targets) Lecture, case study and group discussion. Learning outcomes: L03
Week 8: Mod 3 - Investigation Techniques (Private Sector Targets) Lecture, case study and group discussion. Learning outcomes: L03
Week 9: Mod 3 - Regulations & Responses (Government / Critical Infrastructure Targets) Lecture, case study and group discussion. Learning outcomes: L04
Week 10: Mod 4 - Investigation Techniques (Government / Critical Infrastructure Targets) - Online Only Lecture Pre-Recorded due to King’s Birthday Holiday. Learning outcomes: L04
Week 11: Short Answer Exercise 2 (Mod 3 & Mod 4) - In Class Assessment Short Answer Exercise 2 conducted in class under supervision. Learning outcomes: L03, L04

Week 12: Guest Presenter - Critical Infrastructure Targets Guest presentation discussing Australian strategies to prevent and respond to attacks against critical infrastructure. Learning outcomes: L03, L04
Week 13: Course Conclusion & Review General discussion that will draw together all course learning objectives.
